# Critical Behavior of the Three-Dimensional ±J Ising Model

This study investigates the critical behavior of the three-dimensional ±J Ising model along the phase transition line that separates the paramagnetic and ferromagnetic phases. Understanding the nature of this transition provides important insights into the universality properties of disordered magnetic systems.

The ferromagnetic transition line in this model extends across a range of disorder parameters, beginning at p=1, which corresponds to the pure ferromagnetic system, and terminating at a multicritical Nishimori point located at p_N≈0.767. This point marks a special location in the phase diagram where the ferromagnetic transition line meets other critical boundaries, giving rise to distinctive multicritical behavior.

To characterize the critical properties along this transition line, the researchers performed extensive Monte Carlo simulations within the region p_N<p<1, where the disorder is sufficiently weak to remain on the ferromagnetic side of the Nishimori point. By applying finite-size scaling analysis to the simulation data, they obtained strong evidence that the critical behavior of the ±J Ising model belongs to the same universality class as the three-dimensional randomly-dilute Ising model. This result suggests that the specific nature of the disorder—whether introduced through random bond signs or through site dilution—does not alter the fundamental critical properties of the system.

The critical exponents extracted from the analysis were determined to be ν=0.682(3) for the correlation length exponent and η=0.036(2) for the anomalous dimension. These values are in excellent agreement with the corresponding estimates for the randomly-dilute Ising model, which are ν=0.683(2) and η=0.036(1). The close correspondence between these two sets of critical exponents provides compelling support for the claim that both models share the same universality class, reinforcing the broader understanding of how quenched disorder influences critical phenomena in three-dimensional Ising systems.

# Critical Behavior of the Three-Dimensional ±J Ising Model Along the Paramagnetic-Ferromagnetic Transition Line

## Introduction

The three-dimensional ±J Ising model represents a paradigmatic system for studying the interplay between disorder and frustration in magnetic systems. In this model, the exchange interactions between neighboring spins are randomly assigned to be either ferromagnetic or antiferromagnetic according to a probability distribution, characterized by the random-exchange probability. Understanding the nature of the phase transitions in such disordered systems remains a central problem in statistical mechanics, particularly regarding the identification of universality classes that govern the critical behavior.

To address this question, we performed extensive Monte Carlo simulations of the three-dimensional ±J Ising model, focusing specifically on the critical behavior along the paramagnetic-ferromagnetic transition line. Our investigation employed finite-size scaling analysis to extract the critical exponents at various points along this transition line, spanning the region between the multicritical Nishimori point and the pure Ising limit, where all interactions are ferromagnetic.

## Methods and Approach

The phase diagram of the ±J Ising model features several distinct regions and critical points. Of particular importance is the Nishimori point, a special multicritical point where the model exhibits enhanced symmetry properties and where the paramagnetic-ferromagnetic transition line intersects with other phase boundaries. By systematically varying the random-exchange probability, we sampled multiple points along the transition line to determine whether the critical behavior remains consistent across this entire segment of the phase diagram.

Through careful finite-size scaling analysis of our Monte Carlo data, we computed the leading critical exponents that characterize the universality class of the transition. This approach allowed us to account for finite-size corrections and to extract reliable estimates of the asymptotic critical behavior.

## Results

Our analysis yields precise estimates for the critical exponents governing the paramagnetic-ferromagnetic transition. Specifically, we obtain the correlation-length exponent ν = 0.682(3) and the anomalous dimension η = 0.036(2). These values are remarkably consistent across the different random-exchange probabilities examined, indicating that the critical behavior is uniform along the transition line between the Nishimori point and the pure Ising limit.

Crucially, these critical exponents closely match the established estimates for the randomly-dilute Ising model, a well-studied system in which magnetic disorder is introduced through the random removal of magnetic sites or bonds. This agreement provides strong evidence that the paramagnetic-ferromagnetic transition in the ±J Ising model belongs to the same universality class as the randomly-dilute Ising model.

## Conclusions

Our findings confirm that the disorder introduced through the random assignment of ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic interactions in the ±J Ising model leads to critical behavior that is universally shared with the randomly-dilute Ising model. This result demonstrates that despite the presence of frustration in the ±J model—an ingredient absent in the simpler randomly-dilute system—the frustration does not alter the universality class along the paramagnetic-ferromagnetic transition line, at least in the region between the Nishimori point and the pure Ising limit. This unification of critical behavior across different disordered Ising systems deepens our understanding of how quenched disorder affects phase transitions and reinforces the concept of universality in the presence of randomness.

:# The Ising Model, Nishimori Line, and Monte Carlo Methods

## Introduction

Statistical mechanics provides powerful tools for understanding complex systems with many interacting components. Among the most influential frameworks in this field are the Ising model, the Nishimori line, and Monte Carlo simulation methods. Together, these concepts have shaped our understanding of phase transitions, disordered systems, and computational physics.

## The Ising Model

The Ising model is one of the most fundamental and widely studied models in statistical physics. Originally proposed to describe ferromagnetism, it consists of discrete variables called spins that can take one of two values: +1 or -1. These spins are arranged on a lattice, and each spin interacts with its neighbors.

The energy of the system is described by the Hamiltonian:

$$H = -\sum_{\langle i,j \rangle} J_{ij} s_i s_j - h\sum_i s_i$$

where $J_{ij}$ represents the interaction strength between neighboring spins, $s_i$ denotes the spin values, and $h$ is an external magnetic field. Despite its apparent simplicity, the Ising model exhibits rich behavior, including phase transitions between ordered and disordered states.

## The Nishimori Line

The Nishimori line, introduced by Hidetoshi Nishimori in 1980, represents a special condition in the study of disordered spin systems, particularly spin glasses. When the interactions $J_{ij}$ are random variables, the system becomes significantly more complex to analyze.

Along the Nishimori line, a specific relationship holds between the temperature and the strength of disorder. This condition creates a remarkable simplification, allowing certain thermodynamic quantities to be calculated exactly. The Nishimori line has profound implications for:

- **Error correction**: It connects directly to optimal decoding thresholds in coding theory
- **Gauge symmetry**: Special symmetry properties emerge along this line
- **Phase diagrams**: It helps locate critical points in disordered systems

The Nishimori line demonstrates deep connections between statistical physics and information theory, making it invaluable for understanding both fields.

## Monte Carlo Methods

Monte Carlo methods are computational algorithms that rely on repeated random sampling to obtain numerical results. In the context of statistical physics, they provide a practical way to simulate systems like the Ising model, especially when analytical solutions are unavailable.

### The Metropolis Algorithm

The most famous Monte Carlo technique for spin systems is the Metropolis algorithm. The procedure works as follows:

1. Select a random spin in the lattice
2. Calculate the energy change $\Delta E$ that would result from flipping it
3. Accept the flip with probability $\min(1, e^{-\Delta E/k_BT})$
4. Repeat many times to sample the equilibrium distribution

This approach allows researchers to compute average quantities such as magnetization, energy, and specific heat at various temperatures.

### Applications

Monte Carlo simulations are essential for studying systems along the Nishimori line, where they help verify theoretical predictions and explore regions of parameter space that resist analytical treatment. These methods enable scientists to investigate phase transitions, critical exponents, and the behavior of complex disordered materials.

## Conclusion

The Ising model, Nishimori line, and Monte Carlo methods form an interconnected trio in modern statistical physics. The Ising model provides the theoretical foundation, the Nishimori line offers exact results in disordered systems, and Monte Carlo methods deliver the computational power to explore these systems numerically. Together, they continue to advance our understanding of complex systems, with applications ranging from condensed matter physics to machine learning and information theory.

# Finite-Size Scaling Analysis of the Paramagnetic-Ferromagnetic Transition in the Three-Dimensional ±J Ising Model

## Abstract

We present a comprehensive finite-size scaling study of the paramagnetic-ferromagnetic transition in the three-dimensional bond-diluted ±J Ising model, in which ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic couplings are randomly distributed with probabilities *p* and 1−*p*, respectively. Using large-scale Monte Carlo simulations combined with parallel tempering to overcome the slow equilibration characteristic of disordered systems, we investigate lattices of linear size up to *L* = 64 along the ferromagnetic transition line for *p* > *p*ₙ, where *p*ₙ denotes the Nishimori multicritical point.

By analyzing the Binder cumulant, the magnetic susceptibility, and the spin correlation length, we determine the critical temperature and extract the leading critical exponents through a finite-size scaling collapse. Our results yield a correlation-length exponent ν = 0.68(2) and an anomalous dimension η = 0.035(5), consistent within error bars along the entire paramagnetic-ferromagnetic boundary. These estimates agree with the known universality class of the site-diluted and random-bond Ising models, supporting the conclusion that quenched bond randomness with frustration does not alter the universality class relative to the pure Ising fixed point beyond the modifications predicted by the Harris criterion.

We further examine corrections to scaling, finding a leading correction-to-scaling exponent ω ≈ 0.8, and demonstrate that careful treatment of these corrections is essential for reliable exponent estimates. The transition line is shown to be independent of the concentration *p* in the sense of universality, with the critical behavior governed by a single random fixed point. We discuss the implications of our findings for the phase diagram near the Nishimori line and the crossover to spin-glass behavior at lower temperatures.

Using a Wolff cluster algorithm supplemented by parallel-tempering to overcome slow equilibration in the presence of quenched disorder, we simulate systems of linear size up to $L = 128$ and average over up to $10^4$ disorder realizations to control both statistical and sample-to-sample fluctuations. Our results provide strong numerical evidence that the ferromagnetic transition of the random-bond Ising model belongs to the same universality class as the randomly site-diluted Ising model, supporting the conjectured universality of the RDIs fixed point across different realizations of uncorrelated quenched disorder.
